verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Korba power-sector contractors and O&M/service vendors tied to NTPC Korba and Adani's expansion, structured on receivables and milestone billing; avoid merchant-power traders and any discom-dependent receivable book.
title: Korba Power Generation & Distribution: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Korba is a coal-and-plant town: the cash engine is fuel moving into boilers and power moving out on transmission lines, not the retail meter.** A generator buys coal, burns it, sells units under a long-term PPA or in the merchant market, and collects from the offtaker; a contractor or O&M vendor sells labour, spares and shutdown services to that plant and collects against a running bill. **Value sits in the PPA and the fuel linkage; cash sits in the receivable from the offtaker.** So when a proposal lands, check who the offtaker is and what the payment history is; if the offtaker is a state discom, ask for the last twelve months of actual collection dates, not the invoice dates.

## Where the cash cycle bites
**Counterparty risk is the whole credit here, and the rating evidence is blunt: one generator's average collection period extended to over 400 days in FY25 from 351 days, with debtors at Rs. 5,020 crore as of June 30, 2025 [10].** ICRA's thermal methodology assesses liquidity on cash collections from the counterparty, DSRA availability and working-capital limit utilisation [8]. **Capex is lumpy and front-loaded; working capital is a long tail.** So for any plant-side borrower, take the receivable ageing monthly and the DSRA balance; if collections stretch beyond the sanctioned cycle, ask for the offtaker's latest payment record before renewing.

## What has changed now
**The national demand signal is strong but Korba's local signal is softer: Chhattisgarh electricity demand rose 6.7% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5%, and state GST collections grew 2.4% against India's 6.1% [D].** Meanwhile bank credit is running at +22.9% YoY against activity of +9.5%, a gap of 13.4 pp [D] — money is chasing this sector faster than the units are being sold. **Peer results are genuinely good: Vedanta Power posted record quarterly sales with EBITDA up 45% sequentially and margins at 14.5% [5], and separately reported 122% EBITDA growth to INR 421 crore on revenue of INR 2,908 crore [6].** Adani Power operates 18.33 GW across 13 assets with 95% of capacity tied to long-term PPAs and targets 45 GW by FY 2031-32 [7], and is advancing thermal, hydro and nuclear expansion [1]. Coal India's Q2 FY27 net profit rose 57% YoY to Rs 6,547 crore, though brokers cut targets on volume concerns [4]. **Read this as: the large generators are healthy, the local economy is not keeping pace, and the gap is where bad loans get made.** Note the rating sources [8], [9], [10] carry no visible date and [9] is a 2016-era CRISIL outlook — treat them as structural, not current.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue the plant's service tail, not its balance sheet: shutdown and overhaul contractors, coal-handling and ash-handling operators, spares and consumable suppliers, and transport contractors working for NTPC Korba and the Adani expansion [1][2].** These borrowers have short cycles, milestone billing and a single large counterparty whose payment behaviour is observable. **Avoid merchant-power traders, any borrower whose receivable is a discom with a 400-day collection record [10], and unsecured expansion capex.** Structure on milestone billing with a receivable-backed limit, a DSRA or escrow of collections where the borrower is project-side [8], and a covenant capping receivable days at the sanctioned cycle. **Take every month: receivable ageing by offtaker, bank statement of the collection account, work-order book, and coal or spares inventory.** If the borrower cannot produce offtaker-wise ageing, decline.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the collection account, not the P&L.** A slip in monthly collections against the billing run, rising working-capital limit utilisation [8], or a new short-term loan to fund a receivable are the first tells. **Local demand growing 2.8 pp slower than India [D] means the town's order book will thin before the plant's does.** If a contractor's order book is concentrated in one unit and that unit announces a shutdown deferral, ask for the revised schedule before enhancing.

utilisation above 90% for two months -> ask for the short-term debt purpose and reprice

single-unit concentration above 60% -> seek a second work order or reduce limit
demand growth stays below India's by 2 pp or more -> shift new sanctions to O&M and spares only
DSRA / escrow balance for project-side borrowers (monthly)
balance below the covenanted minimum -> stop disbursement until topped up
